name: Español Starter
description: High-frequency Spanish for someone who studied in Madrid and plans to go back. Peninsular usage, everyday register, no textbook sentences.

entries.definition: OK / got it / sounds good — the most-used word in Spain, full stop.
examples: —Nos vemos a las nueve. —Vale. — “See you at nine.” “OK.”
Vale, vale, ya voy. — “OK, OK, I'm coming.”
conversation: Ana: Te recojo a las nueve, ¿te va bien? — I will pick you up at nine, does that work?
Tú: Vale, nos vemos abajo. — OK, see you downstairs.
entries.note: In Spain this replaces okay in about 90% of conversations. Doubling it (vale, vale) means “yes, fine, enough.” Latin American Spanish uses bueno or listo instead.

entries.definition: How's it going? — the default greeting, more casual than ¿cómo estás?
examples: ¿Qué tal el finde? — “How was the weekend?”
¿Qué tal? ¿Todo bien? — “How's it going? All good?”
conversation: Ana: ¡Hombre, cuánto tiempo! ¿Qué tal? — Hey, long time! How are you?
Tú: Muy bien, ¿y tú? ¿Qué tal el trabajo nuevo? — Really good, and you? How is the new job?
entries.note: Works as a greeting on its own and as “how was...” with any noun attached: ¿qué tal la reunión?, ¿qué tal el vuelo?

entries.definition: Cool, great — Spain-only slang, mild and completely everyday.
examples: Qué guay el sitio, ¿cómo lo encontraste? — “What a cool place, how did you find it?”
Me parece guay. — “Sounds good to me.”
conversation: Tú: Qué guay este sitio, ¿cómo lo encontraste? — This place is so cool, how did you find it?
Ana: Me lo dijo un compañero de curro. — A guy from work told me about it.
entries.note: Safe to use with anyone in Spain; it isn't teen slang. Say it in Mexico and you'll be understood as unmistakably Spanish.

entries.definition: Literally uncle/aunt; in Spain, dude / mate — used constantly between friends.
examples: Tío, no me lo puedo creer. — “Dude, I can't believe it.”
Es una tía muy maja. — “She's a really nice person.”
conversation: Ana: Tío, llevo esperando media hora. — Dude, I have been waiting half an hour.
Tú: Perdona, el metro estaba fatal. — Sorry, the metro was a disaster.
entries.note: Context does all the work — same word means your actual uncle. Only for friends and peers, never a colleague you've just met.

entries.definition: Like / sort of — the filler phrase young Spaniards use constantly.
examples: Fuimos en plan tranquilo, sin hacer mucho. — “We went in a chill way, without doing much.”
Me dijo, en plan, que no le interesaba. — “He told me, like, that he wasn't interested.”
conversation: Ana: ¿Qué hicisteis el finde? — What did you do at the weekend?
Tú: Nada, en plan tranquilo. Un par de cañas y a casa. — Nothing, kind of chill. A couple of beers and home.
entries.note: The Madrid equivalent of “like.” Hearing it is more useful than using it — it'll appear in every conversation under 35.

entries.definition: I mean / that is — used to restate or clarify what you just said.
examples: No puedo el jueves, o sea, sí puedo pero por la tarde. — “I can't Thursday, I mean, I can but in the afternoon.”
O sea, que no vienes. — “So basically, you're not coming.”
conversation: Ana: ¿Entonces no vienes? — So you are not coming?
Tú: Sí voy, o sea, llego tarde pero voy. — I am coming, I mean, I will be late but I am coming.
entries.note: Literally “or it may be.” Enormously common as both a genuine clarifier and pure filler.

entries.definition: By the way — introduces a change of subject.
examples: Por cierto, ¿al final cogiste el piso? — “By the way, did you end up taking the apartment?”
Por cierto, te mandé un correo ayer. — “By the way, I sent you an email yesterday.”
conversation: Tú: Por cierto, ¿al final cogiste el piso de Lavapiés? — By the way, did you end up taking the flat in Lavapiés?
Ana: Sí, me mudo el sábado. — Yes, I move on Saturday.
entries.note: The natural conversational pivot. Not the same as por supuesto, which means “of course” — an easy pair to mix up early on.

entries.definition: Of course / right — agreement, and the standard sound of listening.
examples: —Es que no tenía tiempo. —Claro, claro. — “I just didn't have time.” “Right, of course.”
Claro que sí. — “Absolutely.”
conversation: Ana: Es que no me dio tiempo a terminarlo. — I just did not have time to finish it.
Tú: Claro, claro. No pasa nada. — Right, of course. It is fine.
entries.note: Spaniards say claro throughout a conversation to signal they're following, the way English speakers say “right.” Silence reads as disagreement.

entries.definition: To arrange to meet up — the standard verb for making plans.
examples: ¿Quedamos el sábado a las ocho? — “Shall we meet up Saturday at eight?”
He quedado con Marta en Malasaña. — “I'm meeting Marta in Malasaña.”
conversation: Ana: ¿Quedamos el sábado? — Shall we meet up Saturday?
Tú: Vale, ¿a las ocho en Malasaña? — Sure, eight in Malasaña?
entries.note: One of the highest-value verbs for actually having a social life in Spain. Reflexive quedarse means something different — to stay.

entries.definition: To feel like / to be up for something.
examples: Tengo muchas ganas de volver a Madrid. — “I really want to go back to Madrid.”
No tengo ganas de cocinar hoy. — “I don't feel like cooking today.”
conversation: Ana: ¿Te apetece cenar fuera? — Do you fancy dinner out?
Tú: La verdad es que no tengo ganas de nada hoy. — Honestly I do not feel like anything today.
entries.note: Covers both wanting and looking forward to. Tengo ganas on its own is a complete, very common answer.

entries.definition: To miss someone or something.
examples: Echo de menos las cañas de después del trabajo. — “I miss the after-work beers.”
Te echamos de menos por aquí. — “We miss you around here.”
conversation: Ana: ¿Qué es lo que más echas de menos de Madrid? — What do you miss most about Madrid?
Tú: Las cañas de después del trabajo, sin duda. — The after-work beers, no question.
entries.note: The Spain version. Latin America mostly says extrañar, which is understood in Spain but marks you instantly as having learned elsewhere.

entries.definition: To have just done something — the recent past in one construction.
examples: Acabo de llegar. — “I've just arrived.”
Acabábamos de empezar cuando llamó. — “We had just started when he called.”
conversation: Ana: ¿Dónde estás? — Where are you?
Tú: Acabo de llegar, estoy en la puerta. — I have just arrived, I am at the door.
entries.note: Always followed by an infinitive. Structurally simple and it replaces an awkward workaround learners otherwise reach for.

entries.definition: To usually do something — habitual action built into the verb.
examples: Suelo desayunar fuera los viernes. — “I usually have breakfast out on Fridays.”
No solemos trabajar los sábados. — “We don't usually work Saturdays.”
conversation: Ana: ¿Desayunas en casa? — Do you have breakfast at home?
Tú: Suelo desayunar fuera los viernes. — I usually eat out on Fridays.
entries.note: No clean English equivalent — it packs “usually” into the verb itself. Stem-changes to sueLo, sueLes, sueLe.

entries.definition: To have been (doing something) for a length of time — among many other meanings.
examples: Llevo tres años estudiando español. — “I've been studying Spanish for three years.”
¿Cuánto llevas esperando? — “How long have you been waiting?”
conversation: Ana: ¿Cuánto llevas estudiando español? — How long have you been studying Spanish?
Tú: Llevo tres años, pero con pausas. — Three years, but with breaks.
entries.note: This duration sense is the hardest and most useful one. Llevar also means to carry, to wear, and to take someone somewhere.

entries.definition: To take (an amount of time) — how long something lasts.
examples: ¿Cuánto se tarda de Atocha a Chamberí? — “How long does it take from Atocha to Chamberí?”
No tardo nada, cinco minutos. — “I'll be quick, five minutes.”
conversation: Tú: ¿Cuánto se tarda de Atocha a Chamberí? — How long does it take from Atocha to Chamberí?
Ana: Veinte minutos en metro. — Twenty minutes on the metro.
entries.note: Distinct from tomar (to take an object) and llevar. If it's about elapsed time, it's tardar.

entries.definition: To make the most of something — to take advantage of an opportunity, with no negative connotation.
examples: Aprovecha que estás en Madrid y vete al Prado un martes por la mañana. — “Make the most of being in Madrid and go to the Prado on a Tuesday morning.”
Aprovechando que estamos todos, hablemos del plan. — “Since we're all here, let's talk about the plan.”
conversation: Ana: Estoy dos días en Madrid nada más. — I am only in Madrid for two days.
Tú: Aprovecha y vete al Prado un martes por la mañana. Está vacío. — Make the most of it and go to the Prado on a Tuesday morning. It is empty.
entries.note: Unlike English “take advantage of,” this is warm and positive. ¡Que aproveche! is also what you say before someone eats.

entries.definition: To ask for or order something — request, not question.
examples: Voy a pedir otra caña, ¿tú quieres algo? — “I'm going to order another beer, do you want anything?”
Le pedí un favor y me dijo que sí. — “I asked him a favor and he said yes.”
conversation: Tú: Voy a pedir otra caña, ¿quieres algo? — I am going to order another beer, do you want anything?
Ana: Un vino tinto, gracias. — A red wine, thanks.
entries.note: The classic learner mistake is pedir versus preguntar. Pedir asks for a thing; preguntar asks a question. Ordering food is always pedir.

entries.definition: To take out, get, or withdraw — an enormously flexible everyday verb.
examples: Tengo que sacar dinero antes de cenar. — “I need to take out cash before dinner.”
¿Sacaste las entradas? — “Did you get the tickets?”
conversation: Ana: ¿Llevas efectivo? — Do you have cash?
Tú: No, tengo que sacar dinero antes de cenar. — No, I need to take some out before dinner.
entries.note: Also covers getting a grade, taking a photo, and putting a product out. When in doubt about a verb for “get,” sacar is often right in Spain.

entries.definition: To catch, grab, or get — colloquial Spain, used for objects, buses, jokes, and people.
examples: No pillé el chiste. — “I didn't get the joke.”
Pilla tú las cañas y yo pago la cena. — “You grab the beers and I'll get dinner.”
conversation: Ana: ...y por eso el camarero se rió. — ...and that is why the waiter laughed.
Tú: Perdona, no pillé el chiste. — Sorry, I did not get the joke.
entries.note: Very Spanish and very frequent. ¿Lo pillas? is the everyday way to ask “you follow?”

entries.definition: To find out about something, or to catch what was said.
examples: Me enteré ayer de que se mudan a Barcelona. — “I found out yesterday that they're moving to Barcelona.”
Perdona, no me he enterado. — “Sorry, I didn't catch that.”
conversation: Ana: ¿Sabías que se van a Barcelona? — Did you know they are moving to Barcelona?
Tú: Me enteré ayer. Con este ruido casi no me entero de nada. — I found out yesterday. With this noise I barely catch anything.
entries.note: No me he enterado is the single most useful sentence for a learner in a loud bar — it's about missing what was said, not failing to understand the language.

entries.definition: To realize — for something to dawn on you.
examples: No me di cuenta de que era tan tarde. — “I didn't realize it was so late.”
Cuando te das cuenta, ya llevas cinco años aquí. — “Before you know it, you've been here five years.”
conversation: Ana: Son las dos de la mañana. — It is two in the morning.
Tú: No me había dado cuenta. Mañana madrugo, además. — I had not realised. And I am up early tomorrow.
entries.note: Always with de before a clause. Don't confuse with realizar, which means to carry out or accomplish, not to realize.

entries.definition: To pay attention to someone, or to take their advice.
examples: No le hagas caso, siempre exagera. — “Don't pay any attention to him, he always exaggerates.”
Si me hubieras hecho caso, no estaríamos aquí. — “If you'd listened to me, we wouldn't be here.”
conversation: Ana: Dice que el sitio es carísimo. — He says the place is really expensive.
Tú: No le hagas caso, siempre exagera. — Do not pay attention to him, he always exaggerates.
entries.note: Takes an indirect object: hacer caso a alguien. It's about heeding, not merely hearing.

entries.definition: To be worth it.
synonyms: valer la pena (to be worth it)
examples: Es caro, pero merece la pena. — “It's expensive, but it's worth it.”
No merece la pena discutir por eso. — “It's not worth arguing about that.”
conversation: Ana: Son cuarenta euros por el menú. — It is forty euros for the set menu.
Tú: Es caro, pero merece la pena. Fui el año pasado. — It is expensive, but it is worth it. I went last year.
entries.note: Also heard as valer la pena, which is more common in Latin America. Both are correct in Spain.

entries.definition: To get up very early — one verb for the whole idea.
examples: Mañana madrugo, así que me voy ya. — “I'm up early tomorrow, so I'm heading off.”
Odio madrugar los lunes. — “I hate getting up early on Mondays.”
conversation: Ana: ¿Ya te vas? Si son las once. — You are leaving already? It is eleven.
Tú: Mañana madrugo, tengo una llamada a las siete. — I am up early tomorrow, I have a call at seven.
entries.note: English needs four words for this. It's also a socially recognized excuse to leave a dinner in Spain, where dinners start at 10pm.

entries.definition: To work — colloquial Spain, roughly “to graft.”
examples: Llevo currando desde las siete. — “I've been working since seven.”
Mañana no curro, es festivo. — “I'm not working tomorrow, it's a holiday.”
conversation: Ana: ¿Te vienes a comer? — Coming for lunch?
Tú: No puedo, llevo currando desde las siete y voy fatal. — I cannot, I have been working since seven and I am behind.
entries.note: The noun el curro means the job itself. Informal but not rude — you'd say it to colleagues, not in a job interview.

entries.definition: The company or firm.
examples: Trabajo en una empresa de tecnología financiera. — “I work at a fintech company.”
La empresa está creciendo muy rápido. — “The company is growing very fast.”
conversation: Ana: ¿Dónde trabajas ahora? — Where do you work now?
Tú: En una empresa de tecnología financiera, de crecimiento. — At a fintech company, on growth.
entries.note: Also the root of empresario (entrepreneur/businessperson) and emprender (to start a venture) — a useful family to learn together.

entries.definition: Salary — the regular pay itself.
examples: El sueldo no es alto, pero el trabajo me gusta. — “The salary isn't high, but I like the job.”
Me han subido el sueldo este año. — “They raised my salary this year.”
conversation: Ana: ¿Y qué tal el sitio nuevo? — And how is the new place?
Tú: El sueldo no es alto, pero el trabajo me gusta mucho. — The salary is not high, but I really like the work.
entries.note: El salario is the more formal contractual term; el sueldo is what people actually say. La nómina is the payslip.

entries.definition: To spend money, or to use something up.
examples: Gasto demasiado en cafés, lo sé. — “I spend too much on coffee, I know.”
No quiero gastar más de cincuenta euros. — “I don't want to spend more than fifty euros.”
conversation: Ana: Otro café. — Another coffee.
Tú: Gasto demasiado en cafés, lo sé. — I spend too much on coffee, I know.
entries.note: Only for money and resources. Spending time is pasar tiempo — using gastar there is a common and very audible learner error.

entries.definition: To save money — and by extension, to save time or effort.
examples: Intento ahorrar un poco cada mes. — “I try to save a bit every month.”
Eso nos ahorra dos horas de trabajo. — “That saves us two hours of work.”
conversation: Ana: ¿Cómo lo haces para viajar tanto? — How do you manage to travel so much?
Tú: Intento ahorrar un poco cada mes, sin pensarlo. — I try to save a little every month, without thinking about it.
entries.note: Los ahorros are savings. Different verb from guardar (to keep/store) and salvar (to rescue) — English “save” splits three ways in Spanish.

entries.definition: To invest — money, time, or effort.
examples: Empecé a invertir con veinte euros al mes. — “I started investing with twenty euros a month.”
Hemos invertido mucho tiempo en esto. — “We've invested a lot of time in this.”
conversation: Ana: Invertir suena a cosa de ricos. — Investing sounds like a rich person thing.
Tú: Empecé con veinte euros al mes. En serio. — I started with twenty euros a month. Genuinely.
entries.note: Also means to reverse or invert something, which makes la inversión mean both “investment” and “inversion.” Context separates them cleanly.

entries.definition: The stock market — and also, everyday, a bag.
examples: La bolsa cayó un tres por ciento ayer. — “The market fell three percent yesterday.”
¿Quieres una bolsa? — “Do you want a bag?”
conversation: Ana: ¿Viste que la bolsa cayó ayer? — Did you see the market fell yesterday?
Tú: Un tres por ciento. No pasa nada, es normal. — Three percent. It is fine, that is normal.
entries.note: Same double meaning as English “exchange” having two lives. La Bolsa de Madrid is the actual exchange; una bolsa is what you carry groceries in.

entries.definition: Risk.
examples: Es una inversión de bajo riesgo. — “It's a low-risk investment.”
No quiero correr ese riesgo. — “I don't want to take that risk.”
conversation: Ana: ¿Es seguro esto? — Is this safe?
Tú: Es de bajo riesgo, pero riesgo cero no existe. — It is low risk, but zero risk does not exist.
entries.note: Note the collocation: you run a risk in Spanish (correr un riesgo), not take one. Arriesgado is the adjective for risky.

entries.definition: Debt.
examples: Quiero pagar la deuda de la tarjeta antes de invertir. — “I want to pay off the card debt before investing.”
Está libre de deudas por primera vez. — “She's debt-free for the first time.”
conversation: Ana: ¿Invierto o pago la tarjeta primero? — Should I invest or pay off the card first?
Tú: La deuda de la tarjeta primero, siempre. — The card debt first, always.
entries.note: Deber is both “to owe” and “must,” which is a nice accidental logic. Estar en deuda con alguien means to be indebted to someone personally.

entries.definition: Cheap, inexpensive.
examples: El menú del día es barato y está buenísimo. — “The set lunch is cheap and it's excellent.”
Lo barato sale caro. — “Cheap things end up expensive.”
conversation: Ana: ¿Comemos aquí? — Shall we eat here?
Tú: El menú del día es barato y está buenísimo. — The set lunch is cheap and it is excellent.
entries.note: That second line is a fixed proverb and gets used constantly. Its opposite is caro, and the menú del día really is the best value in Spain.

entries.definition: The bill, or a bank account — same word.
examples: La cuenta, por favor. — “The check, please.”
Abrí una cuenta nueva el mes pasado. — “I opened a new account last month.”
conversation: Tú: Perdona, ¿nos traes la cuenta? — Excuse me, could you bring us the bill?
Camarero: Ahora mismo. — Right away.
entries.note: In Spain the bill never arrives until you ask; waiting politely can go on indefinitely. Also lives inside darse cuenta and tener en cuenta (to bear in mind).

entries.definition: A small draft beer — the standard Spanish pour, around 200ml.
examples: ¿Nos tomamos una caña? — “Shall we grab a beer?”
Dos cañas y una tapa de tortilla, por favor. — “Two beers and a portion of tortilla, please.”
conversation: Ana: ¿Nos tomamos una caña antes de ir? — Shall we have a beer before we go?
Tú: Va, pero una. Mañana madrugo. — Go on, but one. I am up early tomorrow.
entries.note: The small size is the point — you order several across an evening rather than nursing a pint. In Madrid a caña often arrives with a free tapa.

entries.definition: Mobile phone.
examples: Me he dejado el móvil en casa. — “I left my phone at home.”
Te escribo por el móvil luego. — “I'll message you later.”
conversation: Ana: Te he llamado tres veces. — I called you three times.
Tú: Me he dejado el móvil en casa, perdona. — I left my phone at home, sorry.
entries.note: Spain says móvil; Latin America says celular. A small word that immediately signals which Spanish you learned.

entries.definition: Computer.
examples: Trabajo todo el día delante del ordenador. — “I work in front of the computer all day.”
Se me ha estropeado el ordenador. — “My computer's broken.”
conversation: Ana: ¿Trabajas mucho desde casa? — Do you work from home a lot?
Tú: Todo el día delante del ordenador, sí. — All day in front of the computer, yes.
entries.note: From the French ordinateur. Latin America uses computadora — another instant regional marker.

entries.definition: You (plural, informal) — used in Spain and essentially nowhere else.
examples: ¿Vosotros venís esta noche? — “Are you all coming tonight?”
Vosotros sabéis más de esto que yo. — “You lot know more about this than I do.”
conversation: Tú: ¿Vosotros venís esta noche? — Are you all coming tonight?
Ana: Nosotros sí, ellos no lo saben todavía. — We are, they do not know yet.
entries.note: Carries its own verb endings (-áis, -éis). Latin America uses ustedes for everything. Learning vosotros is the price of sounding like you actually lived in Madrid.

entries.definition: I don't mind / it's all the same to me.
synonyms: me da lo mismo (same to me)
examples: —¿Italiano o japonés? —Me da igual, elige tú. — “Italian or Japanese?” “I don't mind, you pick.”
Me da igual la hora, avísame y voy. — “Any time works, let me know and I'll come.”
conversation: Ana: ¿Italiano o japonés? — Italian or Japanese?
Tú: Me da igual, elige tú. — I do not mind, you choose.
entries.note: Tone decides everything: relaxed it means “either is fine,” flat it means “I couldn't care less.” Me da lo mismo is the exact equivalent.
